consumer.headline: Red meat and stroke: no association, or an increased risk?
consumer.why: Claim A asserts that unprocessed red meat consumption has no association with incident stroke, whereas Claim B states that it is associated with an increased risk of stroke.
consumer.verdict_label: Checked by hand against the abstracts: a real disagreement
consumer.verdict_reason: Both are meta-analyses of unprocessed red meat and incident stroke on comparable adult populations; a 2010 pooled null vs a 2016 updated point estimate — the canonical time-updated red-meat disagreement.
consumer.verdict_basis: builder's hand review against the source abstracts (venue, method, population, dose, outcome)
consumer.verdict_doubt: We doubt our own "disagreement" verdict on red meat / stroke: one paper reports no link while the other gives a risk per 100 g a day — the same kind of difference in how results were measured that got the triglyceride pair set aside. The verdict is unchanged; the pair has been added to a packet for expert review (not yet sent).

consumer.headline: Set aside (different measures): Alcohol and heart attack: is the risk-curve the same for men's drinking-days and for weekly totals across populations?
consumer.why: Claim A indicates that the risk reduction for myocardial infarction is similar regardless of alcohol intake level, whereas Claim B asserts a continuous, log-linear decrease in risk with higher alcohol consumption.
consumer.verdict_label: Set aside: the two papers measure different things
consumer.verdict_reason: Different populations (US male health professionals only vs mixed IPD across 19 countries) AND different dose constructs (per-drinking-day vs per-week). The apparent conflict evaporates once the measures are reconciled — a regime-conflation, not a real disagreement.
consumer.verdict_basis: builder's hand review against the source abstracts (venue, method, population, dose, outcome)

consumer.headline: Alcohol and stroke: is there any overall association?
consumer.why: Claim A finds no significant overall association between alcohol consumption and incident stroke, whereas Claim B reports that higher alcohol consumption is linearly associated with an increased stroke risk.
consumer.verdict_label: Checked by hand against the abstracts: a real disagreement
consumer.verdict_reason: Both are meta-analyses of adult drinkers with comparable methods; an older pooled null vs a newer IPD's linear positive slope. Direct disagreement on whether an aggregate association exists.
consumer.verdict_basis: builder's hand review against the source abstracts (venue, method, population, dose, outcome)
consumer.verdict_topic: alcohol / stroke — is there an association?

consumer.headline: Alcohol and ischemic stroke: a J-shaped curve or a straight line?
consumer.why: Claim A asserts a J-shaped curvilinear dose-response relationship between alcohol consumption and stroke risk, whereas Claim B asserts a linear relationship where higher consumption is consistently associated with higher risk.
consumer.verdict_label: Checked by hand against the abstracts: a real disagreement
consumer.verdict_reason: Both meta-analyses on comparable populations; the disagreement is model choice (fractional-polynomial J-shape vs assumed linear). A modelling-choice disagreement on the same construct is a substantive disagreement.
consumer.verdict_basis: builder's hand review against the source abstracts (venue, method, population, dose, outcome)

consumer.headline: Red meat and type-2 diabetes: no association, or an increased risk?
consumer.why: Claim A finds no association between unprocessed red meat intake and incident diabetes, whereas Claim B reports that higher intake of red meat is associated with an increased incidence of type 2 diabetes.
consumer.verdict_label: Checked by hand against the abstracts: a real disagreement
consumer.verdict_reason: Same time-updated red-meat pattern as pair #1: 2010 pooled null vs 2019 umbrella-positive on the same construct.
consumer.verdict_basis: builder's hand review against the source abstracts (venue, method, population, dose, outcome)
consumer.verdict_doubt: We doubt our own "disagreement" verdict on red meat / type 2 diabetes: one paper is about unprocessed red meat and the other about red meat in general, which may not be the same exposure. The verdict is unchanged; the pair has been added to a packet for expert review (not yet sent).

consumer.headline: Alcohol and all-cause mortality: does a protective J-shape survive adjustment for abstainer-bias and study quality?
consumer.why: Claim A asserts that alcohol consumption lowers all-cause mortality risk, whereas Claim B states that higher-quality studies show no such reduction in mortality risk.
consumer.verdict_label: Checked by hand against the abstracts: a real disagreement
consumer.verdict_reason: Same construct (light drinking vs abstention on all-cause mortality) but with Stockwell's abstainer-bias correction applied. The central controversy in alcohol epidemiology; systematic reviews reaching opposite conclusions after quality adjustment.
consumer.verdict_basis: builder's hand review against the source abstracts (venue, method, population, dose, outcome)
consumer.verdict_topic: alcohol / all-cause mortality — J-shape vs quality-adjusted null

consumer.headline: Set aside (duplicate pair): Alcohol and all-cause mortality: does the protective J-shape survive abstainer-bias correction? (restated)
consumer.why: Claim A finds that alcohol consumption significantly reduces all-cause mortality risk, whereas Claim B finds no significant reduction in mortality risk after controlling for abstainer biases and study quality.
consumer.verdict_label: Set aside: duplicate of another pair
consumer.verdict_reason: Same paper pair and same topic as the pair immediately above (BMJ 2011 vs Stockwell 2016 alcohol/mortality). The other Claim B here is a near-identical restatement of the abstainer-bias correction. Counted once.
consumer.verdict_basis: builder's hand review against the source abstracts (venue, method, population, dose, outcome)
consumer.verdict_topic: alcohol / all-cause mortality — duplicate of previous

consumer.headline: Set aside (different measures): Triglycerides and coronary heart disease: a raised risk, or no link once other risk factors are accounted for?
consumer.why: Claim A reports a significant increase in coronary heart disease risk associated with higher triglyceride levels, whereas Claim B finds no significant association after adjusting for conventional risk factors.
consumer.verdict_label: Set aside: the two papers measure different things
consumer.verdict_reason: Different adjustment and contrast: Sarwar 2006's own conclusion says its triglyceride–heart-disease link depends heavily on other risk factors and leaves any independent link open, while the 2009 pooled analysis reports the per-standard-deviation estimate alongside the other blood lipids, so both statements can be true.
consumer.verdict_basis: builder's hand review against the source abstracts (venue, method, population, dose, outcome)
consumer.verdict_topic: triglycerides / coronary heart disease — independent of other risk factors?

consumer.headline: Set aside (duplicate pair): Triglycerides and coronary heart disease: the EPIC-Norfolk cohort estimate (restated)
consumer.why: Claim A reports a statistically significant increased risk of coronary heart disease associated with higher triglyceride levels, whereas Claim B reports no significant association after adjusting for risk factors.
consumer.verdict_label: Set aside: duplicate of another pair
consumer.verdict_reason: Same paper pair and same finding as the triglyceride pair above; the EPIC-Norfolk estimate is one component of Sarwar 2006's pooled result.
consumer.verdict_basis: builder's hand review against the source abstracts (venue, method, population, dose, outcome)
consumer.verdict_topic: triglycerides / coronary heart disease — EPIC-Norfolk estimate (duplicate)

consumer.headline: Set aside (duplicate pair): Triglycerides and coronary heart disease: the Reykjavik cohort estimate (restated)
consumer.why: Claim A finds a significant positive association between triglyceride levels and coronary heart disease risk after adjustment, whereas Claim B finds no significant association.
consumer.verdict_label: Set aside: duplicate of another pair
consumer.verdict_reason: Same paper pair and same finding as the triglyceride pair above; the Reykjavik estimate is one component of Sarwar 2006's pooled result.
consumer.verdict_basis: builder's hand review against the source abstracts (venue, method, population, dose, outcome)

consumer.headline: 4 separate teams ran into the same wall: tested on too few examples
consumer.kind_short: A problem that several independent teams ran into
consumer.kind_long: Papers describe the limits of their own work. When separate teams — who did not build on each other — keep reporting the same limit, that is a sign of a real obstacle rather than one group's bad luck.
consumer.strength_meaning: There is real evidence behind this, but it rests on a small number of papers — read them before trusting it.
consumer.why: 4 separate research teams each reported hitting this in their own work. They did not build on each other, so this is unlikely to be one group's bad luck. Their papers span 1 years. We could read 2 of them in full, which is where teams describe what actually went wrong.

caveats.label: Based partly on summaries only
caveats.text: For some of these papers we only had the summary, not the full text. Papers we could read in full reveal far more about their own limits, so this may be built on an incomplete picture.

caveats.label: Broadly worded
caveats.text: The problem these papers describe is worded broadly enough that they may not be running into quite the same thing.
